q: Which deed gives the buyer the most protection?
wrong: Special warranty covers only the grantor's ownership period.
Quitclaims carry no warranties.
Bargain and sale implies title but gives no warranties against defects.
why: A general warranty deed warrants title against all defects, past and present.

q: A quitclaim deed:
options: Transfers whatever interest the grantor has, with no warranties
Is used only by the government
wrong: Quitclaims guarantee nothing.
Quitclaims can be recorded.
Anyone can use one.
why: A quitclaim releases any interest the grantor may have, without promises.

q: Notarizing a deed (acknowledgment) is required to:
options: Make it valid between the parties
wrong: A deed can be valid without acknowledgment.
Tax bills don't depend on acknowledgment.
Deeds don't create liens.
why: Acknowledgment is typically needed to record, not for validity.

q: Title passes to the grantee when the deed is:
wrong: The grantor signs; the grantee doesn't need to.
Recording gives notice, but title passes on delivery.
A written deed alone doesn't transfer title.
why: Delivery with intent to transfer, plus acceptance, passes title.

q: Who must sign a deed for it to be valid?
wrong: The grantee generally doesn't sign.
Only the grantor's signature is essential.
Escrow doesn't sign the deed.
why: The grantor, who transfers title, must sign.

q: A seller deeds a home to Buyer A, who doesn't record, then deeds it to Buyer B, who pays value, doesn't know about A, and records first. In most states:
options: Buyer B likely has the stronger claim
Buyer A always wins because they were first
wrong: Failing to record can cost a buyer priority against a later good-faith buyer who records.
Recording laws don't create co-ownership here.
The seller conveyed it.
why: Recording laws protect good-faith buyers who record. Always record promptly.

q: Recording a deed gives constructive notice to the public.
wrong: That's the point of recording.
why: True.

q: A special warranty deed warrants title against defects from any time in the property's history.
wrong: A special warranty covers only defects that arose during the grantor's ownership.
why: False.

q: Which is an essential element of a deed?
options: A legal description of the property
wrong: Deeds recite consideration but needn't state the price.
The grantee doesn't need to sign.
Loan details aren't in the deed.
why: The deed must identify the property with a legal description.
hook: No legal description, no valid deed.

q: Your buyer asks which type of deed they should insist on. What should the agent do?
options: Explain the basic differences, and refer the specific legal choice to an attorney or the title company
Tell them a quitclaim is fine
wrong: A quitclaim offers no protection; advising it could hurt the buyer.
Choosing for them is legal advice.
Deed type affects protection.
why: Agents can explain concepts but refer legal decisions.
hook: Know your lane. Refer the rest.

q: The recorded history of ownership of a property is the:
wrong: An abstract of judgment records a court judgment.
A plat map shows lots.
A policy insures title; it isn't the history.
why: The chain of title traces each transfer.
hook: Follow the chain; fix the breaks.

q: A buyer gets a loan, and the lender requires title insurance. The lender's policy protects:
wrong: The lender's policy doesn't protect the owner.
It protects the lender.
The seller isn't insured by it.
why: Buyers need an owner's policy for their own protection.
hook: Lender's policy protects the lender. Buy your own.

q: Title insurance mainly protects against:
options: Covered defects in title that existed before the policy date
wrong: Title insurance looks backward, not forward.
That's property insurance.
Market risk isn't insured.
why: Title insurance covers hidden title problems from the past, like forgery.

q: A lawsuit to resolve competing ownership claims and clear title is a:
wrong: Partition divides co-owned property.
Foreclosure enforces a lien.
A lis pendens is a notice of a lawsuit, not the lawsuit.
why: Quiet title actions clear clouds on title.

q: A title search finds a mortgage paid off in 2010 that was never released. This is a:
wrong: It's a defect, so title isn't clearly marketable until fixed.
An easement is a use right.
An encroachment is a physical intrusion.
why: An unreleased lien casts doubt on title until it's cleared.
hook: Follow the chain; fix the breaks.

q: An owner's title policy generally protects the owner for as long as they or their heirs own the property.
wrong: Owner's coverage continues during ownership.
why: True.
hook: Owner's policy: for as long as you own it.

q: Title insurance is usually paid for monthly, like homeowner's insurance.
wrong: Title insurance is a one-time premium paid at closing.
why: False.
hook: Title insurance: one premium, at closing.

q: A summary of all recorded documents affecting a property is an:
wrong: A policy insures; it doesn't summarize.
Appraisals value property.
Escrow instructions direct the closing.
why: An abstract summarizes the record.

q: Years after closing, a forged deed in the chain of title surfaces and threatens the owner's title. The owner has an owner's title policy. Most likely:
options: The title insurer defends the title and pays covered losses
The lender's policy pays the owner
wrong: Forgery in the chain is a classic covered risk.
The lender's policy protects the lender.
The agent didn't insure title.
why: Owner's policies cover defects like forgeries that existed before the policy date.

q: Marketable title means title reasonably free from doubt, which a prudent buyer would accept.
wrong: That's the standard definition.
why: True.
hook: Marketable: a careful buyer would take it.

q: An escrow agent:
options: Is a neutral party following the parties' written instructions
wrong: Escrow is neutral.
Escrow is neutral.
Escrow doesn't negotiate.
why: Escrow holds funds and documents neutrally per instructions.

q: On a closing statement, a debit to the buyer is:
wrong: That's a credit.
Commission is typically a seller debit.
Not a closing statement concept.
why: Debits are charges; credits are amounts owed to or received by a party.
hook: Debit: you owe. Credit: you get.

q: On a closing statement, the purchase price is:
options: A debit to the buyer and a credit to the seller
A credit to the buyer and a debit to the seller
wrong: That's reversed.
The seller receives the price.
The buyer pays the price.
why: The buyer pays the price (debit), and the seller receives it (credit).
hook: Buyer pays the price; seller gets it.

q: On the closing statement, the buyer's earnest money deposit is:
wrong: The buyer already paid it, so it's credited back.
The seller already counts the full price as a credit.
It must be accounted for.
why: Earnest money was already paid, so it's credited to the buyer.

q: FIRPTA withholding may apply when:
options: The seller is a foreign person
The buyer is a first-time buyer
wrong: Buyer status doesn't trigger FIRPTA.
Construction age doesn't matter.
Price can create exemptions but doesn't trigger it.
why: FIRPTA generally requires withholding when a foreign person sells U.S. real property, unless an exemption applies.

q: The closing agent usually reports a real estate sale to the IRS on Form 1099-S.
wrong: The settlement agent typically files the 1099-S.
why: True.

q: An escrow agent may release funds based on a phone call from one party, without written instructions.
wrong: Escrow acts on written instructions from the parties.
why: False.

q: The seller's existing mortgage payoff shows on the closing statement as a:
wrong: The payoff reduces what the seller receives.
The buyer doesn't pay the seller's loan.
The buyer isn't credited the seller's payoff.
why: Paying off the seller's loan is a charge against the seller.

q: A home sells for $420,000. The seller pays a $23,100 commission, $8,400 in other costs, and a $251,500 loan payoff. What are the seller's net proceeds?
formula: Net proceeds = price − commission − costs − loan payoff
why: Price less all seller debits is $137,000.

q: Your buyer receives the Closing Disclosure and doesn't understand a fee. What should the agent do?
options: Review it with the buyer, and direct loan-fee questions to the lender before closing
Tell them to sign without reading
Tell them all fees are standard
Wait until the closing table to ask
wrong: Clients should understand what they sign.
Not all fees are standard or correct.
The three-day window exists for review.
why: Help the client review it and get answers from the lender in time.
hook: Three days to review before close.

q: A foreclosure carried out by a trustee's sale, without a court case, is:
wrong: Judicial foreclosure goes through court.
Strict foreclosure gives title to the lender without a sale and is rare.
Partition divides co-owned property.
why: A deed of trust's power of sale allows nonjudicial foreclosure.
hook: Deed of trust: the trustee can sell.

q: A sale where the lender agrees to accept less than the loan balance is a:
wrong: REO is lender-owned after foreclosure.
A deed in lieu transfers the property to the lender.
A wraparound is a financing structure.
why: In a short sale, the lender approves a payoff less than what's owed.
hook: Short sale: the lender takes less.

q: Which is required for adverse possession?
options: Open, continuous, hostile and exclusive possession for the statutory period
wrong: Permission defeats the hostile requirement.
Paying rent shows permission.
No deed is involved.
why: Adverse possession requires use that's open, continuous, hostile, and exclusive for the time the law sets.

q: A person who dies without a valid will dies:
wrong: Testate means with a will.
A devise is a gift by will.
Escheat happens only if there are no heirs.
why: Without a will, state law decides who inherits.

q: A 1031 exchange allows an investor to:
options: Defer taxes on gain by exchanging investment property for like-kind property
Avoid taxes forever on a primary home
wrong: 1031 applies to investment or business property, and defers rather than eliminates.
Property taxes aren't affected.
Commissions aren't affected.
why: 1031 exchanges defer capital gains tax on like-kind investment property.
hook: Swap like for like, defer the tax.

q: A married couple who lived in their home for 4 of the last 5 years sells it with a $590,000 gain. Under the home sale exclusion, how much of the gain may be taxable?
formula: Taxable gain = total gain − exclusion ($500,000 for most married couples filing jointly)
why: Up to $500,000 can be excluded, leaving $90,000.

q: REO refers to property a lender owns after foreclosure.
wrong: REO means real estate owned by the lender.
why: True.

q: The equity of redemption lets a borrower stop foreclosure by paying what's owed before the sale.
wrong: That's the equity of redemption.
why: True.
hook: Pay before the sale, keep the house.

q: A seller behind on payments asks you to list as a short sale. What should the agent do?
options: Explain the process, get lender approval steps started, and recommend the seller see an attorney and tax advisor about deficiency and tax effects
Promise the lender will forgive everything
Tell them to stop all communication with the lender
wrong: You can't promise lender decisions.
Forgiven debt can have tax effects.
Cutting off the lender hurts the short sale.
why: Short sales raise legal and tax questions; refer those while managing the sale.
hook: Know your lane. Refer the rest.

q: A borrower voluntarily deeds the property to the lender to avoid foreclosure. This is a:
wrong: A short sale sells to a third party.
Quiet title resolves competing claims.
Novation substitutes a contract.
why: A deed in lieu transfers the property to the lender instead of foreclosure.
hook: Hand back the keys by deed.

q: A property manager acting under a management agreement is usually a:
wrong: Managers handle many ongoing tasks.
Authority is limited to managing the property.
The manager represents the owner.
why: Ongoing authority over a range of tasks makes a general agent.

q: A property manager's primary goal is generally to:
options: Protect the property and maximize the owner's net income
Keep rents as low as possible
wrong: Low rents may hurt the owner's income.
Poor tenants can cost more.
Deferred maintenance erodes value.
why: Managers balance income and the property's long-term value.
hook: Protect the property, maximize the income.

q: Scheduling annual HVAC servicing before problems occur is:
wrong: Corrective maintenance fixes broken things.
Construction adds improvements.
Deferred maintenance is put off.
why: Preventive maintenance heads off problems.

q: Buying liability insurance to cover slip-and-fall claims is which risk strategy?
wrong: Avoiding would mean eliminating the activity.
Retaining means accepting the cost yourself.
Controlling means reducing risk, like adding handrails.
why: Insurance moves the financial risk to an insurer.

q: Fair housing laws apply to tenant screening.
wrong: Screening criteria must be applied equally and lawfully.
why: True.
hook: Screen fairly, screen everyone the same.

q: Regular financial reports to the owner are part of a property manager's job.
wrong: Accounting to the owner is a fiduciary duty.
why: True.

q: A manager earns 8% of collected rent. A 20-unit building rents each unit at $1,250 a month and collects from 18 units this month. What is the manager's fee?
formula: Fee = units collected × rent × fee rate
why: 8% of $22,500 collected is $1,800.

q: A rental applicant with a disability asks to keep an emotional support animal in a no-pets unit and has proper documentation. What should the property manager do?
options: Treat it as a reasonable accommodation request and process it under fair housing rules
Deny it under the no-pets rule
Steer them to a different property
wrong: Refusing a reasonable accommodation can be discrimination.
Assistance animals aren't pets; pet fees generally don't apply.
That's steering.
why: Assistance animal requests are reasonable accommodation requests.

q: An operating budget for a rental property projects:
options: Expected income and expenses for the year
wrong: Value comes from an appraisal.
Personal taxes aren't part of it.
Leases set terms; the budget projects finances.
why: Budgets plan the year's income and costs.
hook: Plan the money before you spend it.

q: A management agreement should spell out:
options: The manager's authority, duties, fees, and the term
wrong: Tenant data isn't part of the owner-manager contract.
Zoning isn't a contract term.
Irrelevant to the agreement.
why: The agreement defines the agency relationship and compensation.

q: In a gross lease, who usually pays the property's operating expenses?
wrong: That's a net lease.
There's no automatic split.
Managers pay expenses from owner funds, not personally.
why: Gross leases charge fixed rent; the owner pays expenses.

q: In a triple net lease, the tenant pays rent plus:
wrong: Triple net covers more than utilities.
Tenants don't pay the owner's loan directly.
That's a gross lease.
why: The three nets are taxes, insurance, and maintenance.

q: A store's lease requires $4,000 a month base rent plus 5% of annual gross sales over $600,000. Annual sales are $840,000. What is the total annual rent?
formula: Total rent = base rent × 12 + (sales − threshold) × percentage
why: Base plus percentage rent totals $60,000.
hook: Base plus a share of sales.

q: A long-term lease of land on which the tenant builds is a:
wrong: A gross lease concerns who pays expenses.
A percentage lease concerns sales-based rent.
Periodic tenancies renew period to period.
why: Ground leases cover land only, often for decades.
hook: Lease the ground, build on it.

q: A tenant subleases their apartment for three months. If the subtenant doesn't pay, who owes the landlord?
wrong: The lease is still in force.
The landlord's contract is with the original tenant.
The manager isn't liable for rent.
why: In a sublease, the original tenant stays liable to the landlord.
hook: Sublease: you're still on the hook.

q: A lease assignment transfers the tenant's entire remaining interest in the lease.
wrong: That's the difference from a sublease.
why: True.
hook: Assign it all, or sublet a piece.

q: Residential apartment leases are commonly gross leases.
wrong: Tenants usually pay fixed rent; owners cover taxes and insurance.
why: True.

q: A lease with rent that increases on a set schedule is a:
wrong: Gross describes who pays expenses.
Net describes who pays expenses.
Ground describes leasing land.
why: Graduated (step-up) leases raise rent at set intervals.

q: A lease that adjusts rent according to a published measure, like the Consumer Price Index, is an:
wrong: Percentage leases follow sales.
Gross is about expenses.
Ground is about land.
why: Index leases tie rent changes to an index.

q: A landlord sells a building where tenants have one-year leases. The leases generally:
options: Continue, and the new owner takes subject to them
wrong: Sale doesn't end leases.
The terms stay the same.
Nothing ends them automatically.
why: Buyers take the property subject to existing leases.

q: A landlord tries to evict a tenant shortly after the tenant reports code violations to the city. This is likely:
options: Allowed if the lease is month-to-month
wrong: Constructive eviction is caused by the landlord's failure to keep the place usable.
Retaliation is prohibited regardless of lease type.
No law requires it.
why: Landlords can't evict in retaliation for tenants exercising legal rights.

q: A landlord ignores a broken heating system all winter and the unit becomes unlivable. The tenant moves out. This may be:
options: Abandonment by the tenant without excuse
wrong: Retaliation involves the landlord punishing a tenant.
The landlord's failure may excuse the tenant.
Assignment transfers the lease.
why: When a landlord's failure makes the property unusable, the tenant may treat it as an eviction.

q: To remove a tenant who won't pay, a landlord must generally:
wrong: Lockouts are illegal self-help.
Utility shutoffs are illegal self-help.
Removing belongings is illegal self-help.
why: Evictions must go through the legal process.
hook: Evict through court, not the hardware store.

q: The covenant of quiet enjoyment protects the tenant's right to:
options: Use the property without interference from the landlord
wrong: It's not about noise from neighbors.
It doesn't excuse rent for ordinary noise.
Tenants don't choose neighbors.
why: Quiet enjoyment means possession free of the landlord's interference.
hook: Quiet enjoyment: the landlord stays out of the way.

q: A tenant's security deposit is held for the tenant and returned less lawful deductions.
wrong: Deposits belong to the tenant subject to the lease and the law.
why: True. Nevada's deadlines are covered in the state units.
hook: Held for someone else? It's trust money.

q: Most states impose an implied warranty of habitability on residential landlords.
wrong: Landlords must keep homes fit to live in.
why: True.
hook: Habitable, quiet, and no payback evictions.

q: As property manager, you receive a tenant's written request about a leaking water heater. What should the agent do?
options: Respond promptly, arrange the repair under the management agreement, and document it
Ignore it until the lease renews
Tell the tenant to fix it themselves
wrong: Delay can damage the property and breach habitability duties.
Major systems are generally the landlord's duty.
Retaliation is prohibited.
why: Prompt, documented repairs protect the tenant, the owner, and the property.
hook: Prevent before you repair; document both.

q: A tenant with an estate for years dies halfway through the lease. Generally the lease:
options: Converts to a tenancy at will
wrong: Leases for a fixed term generally survive death.
No conversion happens.
Recording isn't required.
why: A lease for a fixed term is generally binding on the estate.

q: Which rental ad is lawful?
options: "2-bed apartment, close to schools and parks"
wrong: Excludes familial status unless qualifying senior housing.
Shows a religious preference.
Discriminates by disability.
why: Describe the property, not who should live there.
hook: Describe the property, not the people.

q: Landlords generally must give reasonable notice before entering a tenant's unit, except in emergencies.
wrong: Notice requirements protect quiet enjoyment; Nevada's specifics are in the state units.
why: True.
